title: Food Safety Basics

sections.heading: Overview
sections.text: Foods can sometimes be contaminated with germs that can make you sick. You may swallow these germs when:

sections.heading: Overview
sections.text: Eating foods that aren't cooked properly

sections.heading: Overview
sections.text: Germs from food spread to your hands, surfaces, or other foods (called cross-contamination)

sections.heading: Overview
sections.text: Food is not refrigerated properly after cooking

sections.heading: Overview
sections.text: There are many different types of foodborne germs that can cause illness, hospitalization, and even death. Some examples include Salmonella, norovirus, and Campylobacter.

sections.heading: Signs and symptoms
sections.text: Signs and symptoms of food poisoning depend on the type of germ you swallowed. The most common symptoms include diarrhea, stomach pain or cramps, nausea, vomiting, and fever.

sections.heading: Riskier foods
sections.text: Some foods are more likely to contain harmful germs, including:

sections.heading: Riskier foods
sections.text: Raw or undercooked poultry, meat, seafood, or eggs

sections.heading: Riskier foods
sections.text: Raw or undercooked sprouts

sections.heading: Riskier foods
sections.text: Unwashed fruits and vegetables

sections.heading: Riskier foods
sections.text: Cut melon

sections.heading: Riskier foods
sections.text: Unpasteurized milk, juice, cider, or soft cheese

sections.heading: Riskier foods
sections.text: Raw dough or raw batter made with uncooked flour

sections.heading: People at risk
sections.text: Anyone can get food poisoning, but certain groups of people are more likely to get very sick from foodborne germs:

sections.heading: People at risk
sections.text: People 65 and older

sections.heading: People at risk
sections.text: Children under 5 years old

sections.heading: People at risk
sections.text: People with weakened immune systems

sections.heading: People at risk
sections.text: Pregnant women

sections.heading: Reducing risk
sections.text: The best ways to avoid food poisoning include:

sections.heading: Reducing risk
sections.text: Washing your hands and surfaces often, including rinsing fresh fruits and vegetables.

sections.heading: Reducing risk
sections.text: Separating riskier foods, like raw meat and eggs, from other foods to avoid cross-contamination.

sections.heading: Reducing risk
sections.text: Cooking food to the right temperature to kill germs.

sections.heading: Reducing risk
sections.text: Refrigerating food promptly after cooking and thawing frozen food safely (not on the counter).

sections.heading: Reducing risk
sections.text: Choosing safer foods, especially if you're more likely to get sick from foodborne germs.

sections.heading: Quick facts
sections.text: CDC estimates that each year 48 million people get sick from a foodborne illness, 128,000 are hospitalized, and 3,000 die.

sections.heading: What CDC is doing
sections.text: CDC helps make food safer by working with partners to track and investigate foodborne illness, identify sources of illness, and determine the best ways to prevent foodborne illness.
